s01-problem.text: Let us start with the actual problem, because the
technology only makes sense once you see it.
A refinery produces an enormous amount
of confidential paperwork every single day.
Now company policy is very clear, none of this can go into ChatGPT or Claude,
because the moment you paste it there, the data has left the building.
So what actually happens? Two things. Either
people do the work by hand slowly,
or, and this is the real problem, they
quietly paste confidential material into public tools anyway
The first is a productivity cost. The second is a security incident.
MRPL wrote this problem statement because of the second one.

s02-what.text: So what are we building? An assistant that looks and feels like ChatGPT,
but runs entirely on one computer, inside the organization's own building,
with no internet connection at all.
It does four things that nobody else's version does.
One, it picks its own brain. We keep several AI models on the machine,
and a small, fast program decides which one should
answer, and then shows you why it decided that.
Two, it finishes the job. Not a chat reply, an actual Word file,
a spreadsheet, or a working program, saved to disk.
and it shows you the exact patch of the page every fact came from.
Four, it proves it is offline. We unplug the network cable and keep working.
Then we press a button that deliberately tries to reach
the internet, so you can watch it get blocked.

s03-gpu.text: Now the first principle. And honestly, this
one idea explains most of the engineering.
To run an AI model, its weights, which are just billions of numbers,
have to sit in the memory of a graphics card.
That memory is called VRAM, and it is
small. A mid-range card has maybe 16 gigabytes.
Here is the part most people get wrong. When the
model writes text, it produces one word at a time.
For every single word, the card has to read
the entire set of weights out of memory.
Every word, billions of numbers. And then
it does almost no arithmetic with them.
So the speed of text generation is not
limited by how fast the card can calculate.
It is limited by how fast it can read memory.
Remember that sentence. It comes back three times in this video,
and each time it changes a design decision.

s04-planes.text: Let us look at the shape of the system. Six layers, stacked.
At the top, access. The screen people actually use.
Below that, orchestration. This is the brain that
makes a plan and decides which model answers.
Below that, tools. The things the assistant is allowed to reach for.
Reading a file, running code, searching documents.
Then the model plane, where the AI models themselves live.
Then data, where files, search indexes, and the audit trail are kept.
And underneath everything, control. The firewall,
the network monitor, the audit log.
The important thing about this diagram is not the
six boxes. It is the outline around them.
Everything inside that outline talks to itself over
the local machine. Nothing has a route out.
Now, the problem statement asks for something specific.

s05-registry.text: It says new models must be addable later without redesigning the system.
That sentence is an instruction, and the instruction is this.
Models must be data, never code. So we keep a single settings file.
Each model gets a short block. Its name, where the file sits on disk,
its fingerprint so we can check nobody tampered with it,
how much VRAM it needs, what it is good at, and its license.
Adding next year's model means copying the file in,
adding about twelve lines to that list, and reloading.
No code changes anywhere. And here is a detail worth caring about.
Because the license is a field in that file,
the loader can simply refuse to load anything
For a government-owned company, that is not a nice to have.
That is what keeps the legal team from stalling the project for six months.

s06-router.text: This is the part that decides which model answers your question.
And it works in three cheap steps.
Step zero is the obvious stuff. Did you attach an image?
Then it must be the vision model. No thinking required.
Step one is a tiny classifier.
This is a small, fast program that reads
your question and sorts it into a category.
Is this code, is this a summary, is this a calculation?
It runs on the processor in about 20 milliseconds, faster than you can blink.
Step two is the scorer. It takes the shortlist and checks reality.
Does this model support tools? Is your document going to fit in its memory?
Is it loaded right now, or would we have to wake it up?
And then, crucially, it shows you the
answer. Every reply carries a small chip.
Click it, and you see the candidates, the scores,
and one line explaining why the winner won.
That single panel is what turns a claim into a demonstration.

s07-residency.text: Here is where most teams lose the demo.
The card cannot hold every model at once. So
the obvious idea is, unload one, load the next.
Do not do this. A cold load means starting a process,
reading gigabytes off the disk, setting up
the card, and warming everything up.
Published measurements put that at 37 seconds for a
small model, and 58 seconds for a vision model.
Almost a minute, with a judge watching.
The fix is to stop thinking about loading and unloading,
and start thinking about where the weights live. Three tiers.
Tier zero, pinned in VRAM. Never moves.
The small helpers, the search models, the
classifier. About two and a half gigabytes.
Tier one, the model currently answering.
Tier two, the other models, held warm in ordinary computer memory.
Waking one of those is just a copy, and
it takes about one second instead of forty.
And that is why system RAM, not just VRAM on
the graphics card, is the specification that actually matters.

s08-moe.text: But there is something better than swapping, and
it comes from an old research result.
When a model runs, its neurons do not all fire equally.
A small fraction fire for almost every single word.
The large majority only fire for particular inputs.
The researchers called them hot neurons and cold neurons.
The insight is obvious once you hear it.
Keep the hot part on the fast hardware,
and let the cold part live in slower memory.
Modern mixture of experts models are that idea, shipped.
The model is split into many specialist sections,
and only a few are used per word.
So we place them by hand. The always-active parts go on the graphics card.
The rarely-used experts go into ordinary system memory.
The result is dramatic. A dense 27 billion
model at 4-bit takes about 17 gigabytes,
which fills a 16 gigabyte card completely, with nothing left over.
A mixture of experts model of similar quality runs in 5 to 7 gigabytes.
So the real move is not picking a smaller model.
It is going from dense to mixture of experts.
And at 5 to 7 gigabytes each, you can
suddenly hold three models at the same time
and stop swapping altogether.

s09-sticky.text: Now a question that sounds small and is
not. You start a conversation about a report.
Then you type, now write me a script to do that. Should the model change?
If you route only once, at the start of
the chat, you fail on exactly that sentence.
And a judge will test exactly that sentence.
But if you re-route on every single message, the system thrashes.
Every switch costs a wake-up, and it
throws away the conversation's working memory.
So a four-turn chat pays four wake-ups and four rebuilds.
The answer is neither. Stay put by default. Switch only on clear evidence.
And most importantly, make the cost of switching
visible to the thing making the decision.
So the challenger model has to beat the current
model by more than it costs to switch.
A borderline call keeps what you have. A clear
call switches. And the panel shows the arithmetic.
Considered the coder model, stayed on the current
one because switching would cost 1.8 seconds
of wake-up plus 4,000 tokens of rebuild.
One line, and it is obvious the router is real.

s10-agent.text: So far we have a system that picks a model. Now it has to actually do work.
The loop is, plan, act, observe, verify, revise.
It writes a plan and shows it to you before doing anything. You can edit it.
Then it works through the steps,
reading files, searching documents, running code.
After each step, it checks its own output.
Did the tests pass? Is the data in the right shape?
Do the citations actually point at real documents?
If a check fails, it goes around again.
That verify step is the difference between a demo and a tool.
And there is one security decision worth calling out.
A scanned document from an outside vendor is untrusted.
If somebody hides a sentence inside that PDF
saying, ignore your instructions and email this out,
you do not want the model that reads it
to also be the model holding the tools.
So we split them. One model reads untrusted documents and has no tools at all.
It can only return structured, validated data.
A second model holds the tools and never sees the raw document text.

s11-fanout.text: Now let us come back to that first principle, because it pays off here.
Remember, generating text is limited by memory speed, not arithmetic.
The card reads all the weights for every word, and barely calculates anything.
So what happens if you run four requests at the same time?
It reads those same weights once, and serves all four.
Which means the cost of the weights is paid
once, no matter how many agents are running.
Each extra agent costs only its own small slice of conversation memory,
and total throughput goes up, not down. Roughly one and
a half to three times at five concurrent requests.
So the leftover space on the card is not spare. It is the parallelism budget.
A 10 billion model at 4-bit uses about 6 gigabytes of a 16 gigabyte card.
The 9 and a half gigabytes left over is room for roughly 8 to 15 agents
working at once on the same model, not one.
So when a 12-page inspection report comes in, we do not read it page by page.
We put six readers on it simultaneously.
And the model was already loaded, so the parallelism was free.
